reference.title: Band Seated Shoulder Press
reference.listing: Video (movement reference; the page could not be fetched from the authoring environment (proxy refused gymvisual.com), so the data sheet was not read; the movement is taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice)

breathing.pattern: Breathe in at the bottom and brace, breathe out as you press up against the band; breathe in as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1.5 s up, short pause, about 2 s down

prescription.load: Band tension is user-chosen (bands are colour-coded by tension): pick one you can move for the target reps with 1-3 reps in reserve; step the feet farther forward on the band, or choke up on it, for more tension.
prescription.progression: More reps, a slower return, a shorter band length under the feet (more stretch), then the next band up.

cues.text: Back pad nearly upright, back against the pad, head neutral. Stand the band under the balls of both feet, feet flat a little ahead of the knees; a handle at each shoulder, palms forward, elbows under the wrists.
Breathe out and press up and slightly in against the band, over the shoulders.
Arms nearly straight overhead, ribs down; the band is at its tightest here, so hold it steady.
Lower under control in about 2 s, elbows tracking under the wrists, a little in front of the body; do not let the band pull you down.
Pause with the hands at shoulder height, band still taut, and repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Arching the low back off the pad at the top, where the band is heaviest
mistakes.fix: Keep the back on the pad and the ribs down; use a lighter band.

mistakes.mistake: Elbows flaring straight out to the sides or drifting behind the body
mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows a little in front of the shoulders (scapular plane) and under the wrists.

mistakes.mistake: Feet lifting or the band slipping off the feet
mistakes.fix: Keep the band under the balls of the feet and the feet flat and planted.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the band snap the hands down

kinematics.norm: Seated presses are usually done with the back pad at 80-90 degrees (clinical opinion)
From about 80-90 degrees at the bottom (upper arm about level) to about 160-170 degrees overhead (clinical opinion)
About 90 degrees at the bottom (forearm vertical) to nearly straight at the top (clinical opinion)
Elbows about 20-40 degrees in front of the frontal plane (scapular plane, about 40 degrees in Tsuruike 2019) rather than straight out to the sides (clinical opinion)
Under the feet, so tension rises as the hands go up and is highest at the top; elastic resistance can give muscle activity comparable to free weights in shoulder exercises (Andersen 2010)
Controlled, about 2 s down and 1-2 s up (clinical opinion)

cautions: Check the band for nicks or tears before every session and replace a worn band; a band that snaps can hit the face or eyes.
Anchor the band to something that cannot move or slip (a rack upright, a heavy bench frame or under the feet) and make sure it is secure before loading it.
Band tension rises as it stretches, so the load is lightest at the start and heaviest at the end of the push; let it return under control rather than snapping back.
Stop if sharp pain, a pinching feeling in the front or top of the shoulder, numbness or tingling occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Shoulder pain overhead: press with palms facing each other (neutral grip) and the elbows further forward, and stop the press short of full overhead.
Low-back discomfort: keep the pad upright and the back against it; do not lean back to finish reps.
regressions: One arm at a time with the other hand on the thigh.
progressions: Stronger band, or shorter band length under the feet.
Standing band shoulder press (more core demand; standing raised deltoid and core activity with dumbbells, Saeterbakken 2013 and 2012).

muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Main shoulder flexor-abductor of the press. The shoulder press gave the highest anterior deltoid activity of four common upper-body exercises (Campos 2020).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: Main shoulder flexor-abductor of the press. The shoulder press gave the highest anterior deltoid activity of four common upper-body exercises (Campos 2020).
muscleNotes.lat_deltoid_r: Lifts the upper arm out and up. Medial deltoid activity in the press was close to that in the lateral raise (Campos 2020); seated was about 15% lower than standing with dumbbells (Saeterbakken 2013).
muscleNotes.lat_deltoid_l: Lifts the upper arm out and up. Medial deltoid activity in the press was close to that in the lateral raise (Campos 2020); seated was about 15% lower than standing with dumbbells (Saeterbakken 2013).
muscleNotes.triceps_r: Straightens the elbow in the top half of the press.
muscleNotes.triceps_l: Straightens the elbow in the top half of the press.
muscleNotes.upper_traps_r: Upward rotation and elevation of the shoulder blade as the arms go overhead.
muscleNotes.upper_traps_l: Upward rotation and elevation of the shoulder blade as the arms go overhead.
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Upward rotation and protraction of the shoulder blade, so the arm can reach fully overhead.
muscleNotes.serratus_l: Upward rotation and protraction of the shoulder blade, so the arm can reach fully overhead.
muscleNotes.pec_r: The clavicular head helps the anterior deltoid at the bottom, when the elbows are forward.
muscleNotes.pec_l: The clavicular head helps the anterior deltoid at the bottom, when the elbows are forward.
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_r: Steadies the shoulder; much less active than the front and side heads, and lower seated than standing (Saeterbakken 2013).
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_l: Steadies the shoulder; much less active than the front and side heads, and lower seated than standing (Saeterbakken 2013).
muscleNotes.infraspinatus_r: Rotator cuff: keeps the ball of the shoulder centred in the socket as the arm rises.
muscleNotes.infraspinatus_l: Rotator cuff: keeps the ball of the shoulder centred in the socket as the arm rises.
muscleNotes.core: Holds the trunk still against the pad. Core activity was lower seated than standing (Saeterbakken 2012).
